claim: Anthropic has been valued at [close to $1 trillion] [as of mid-2026]
quote: Anthropic has been valued at close to $1 trillion
evidence: Anthropic closed a Series H at a $965B valuation (May 28, 2026), widely reported as 'nears $1 trillion'; prediction markets put ~87.5% odds on Anthropic crossing $1T by Dec 31 2026. $965B is close enough to $1T that the claim holds.

claim: Anthropic's annualized revenue was [in the low single billions] in [January 2025]
quote: In January of last year, its annualized revenue was in the low single billions.
evidence: The only reachable figure is a social-media tracker post: ~$1B annualized in January 2025 (rising to $3B by May, $8-10B by December). $1B sits at the very bottom edge of 'low single billions' — directionally right, but the only source is an unaudited individual tracker (tier 4), which caps the verdict.

claim: By [May 2026], Anthropic's annualized revenue run rate was reported at [$47 billion]
quote: By this May, it reported $47 billion.
evidence: $47B run-rate was disclosed alongside Anthropic's May 28, 2026 Series H announcement and reported consistently across outlets.

claim: As of [late July 2026], third-party trackers put Anthropic's annualized revenue at [around $74 billion]
quote: currently put Anthropic at around $74 billion of annualized revenue
evidence: Contemporaneous (pre-video) tracker estimates for July 2026 ranged $69-74.1B, matching the claim. Caveat: Anthropic's own later disclosure (Aug 17, after this video) put the actual run rate at $65B — trackers overshot by ~14% — but the claim is specifically attributed to trackers, not to Anthropic, so it holds as stated.

claim: Anthropic's annualized-revenue growth slowed from [roughly 51% month-over-month] in [May 2026] to [roughly 8% month-over-month] by [July 2026], per third-party trackers
quote: growing at roughly 51% per month per month
evidence: Independent analysis describes month-over-month growth 'cooling from roughly 55% in the spring to the mid-single digits by July' — directionally matches the claimed 51%→8% deceleration, though the exact percentages aren't independently pinned to one source.

claim: Weekly third-party tracker revisions of Anthropic's annualized revenue moved [$54 billion in late May], [$67 billion in early June], [$70 billion in mid-June], then down, then [$71 billion], then [$74 billion] [through July 2026]
quote: 54 billion in late May, 67 in early June, 70 in mid-June, then a wobble backwards, then 71, then 74.
evidence: Independent tracker posts corroborate the shape of this chart: ~$53.2B as of May 2026 (named tracker), climbing to $69-74B by late July across multiple trackers — closely matching the cited progression.

claim: [Roughly $3-4 trillion] has [already] been poured into the American AI industry [as of mid-2026] — data centers, chips, power deals
quote: somewhere between three and four trillion dollars has reportedly been poured into the American AI industry
evidence: $3T+ and $3.6T figures exist, but they describe the total projected buildout cost (Morgan Stanley put $3.6T as the financing requirement for 2026-2030), not money already spent. Actual 2025-2026 hyperscaler capex is closer to $600B for 2026 alone plus prior years — real cumulative spend to date is well short of $3-4T. The claim presents a forward-looking total as already 'poured in.'

claim: The majority of the [$3-4 trillion poured into American AI] is [reportedly] debt — corporate bonds, borrowed money
quote: the majority of it is reportedly debt, corporate bonds, borrowed money
evidence: Debt financing is large and growing fast (hyperscaler bond issuance ran ~4x the historical average in 2025 and is on pace to double again in 2026), but Goldman Sachs projects debt will fund 'more than a third' of AI spending by 2027 — a substantial minority, not a stated majority. No source found supports debt as already exceeding half of total AI spending.

claim: On [$2-3 trillion] of AI-industry debt at a [3-4%] corporate bond rate, interest alone comes to [roughly $100 billion] a year
quote: the interest alone works out to roughly 100 billion
evidence: Arithmetic checks out: $2.5T x 3.5% ≈ $87.5B, in the range of 'roughly $100B.' But the $2-3T debt-stock premise isn't supported by current data — actual AI-related debt issuance found totals roughly $700-800B cumulative through 2025-2026 (hyperscaler bonds ~$121B in 2025, ~$250-300B projected for 2026, plus ~$200B+ private credit), an order of magnitude below $2-3T. The interest figure rests on a debt total the industry has not yet reached.

claim: Most of the big AI labs [reportedly] lose money on every single request served [as of 2026]
quote: most of the big labs reportedly lose money on every single request served
evidence: Was true in 2024 (Anthropic's gross margin was -94%). By 2026 the picture reversed: Anthropic's API gross margin exceeds 80% (blended ~44-60%), and OpenAI's gross margin improved to ~39% in Q1 2026 — meaning marginal requests are no longer loss-making at current pricing, even though both companies remain net-loss overall on R&D/opex. The claim conflates net unprofitability (real) with per-request loss (outdated for 2026).

claim: To produce [$100 billion] in profit at a [10%] margin, the AI industry needs [roughly $1 trillion] of revenue a year
quote: the AI industry needs to generate roughly 1 trillion dollars of revenue every year
evidence: Pure arithmetic: $100B / 10% = $1T — correct. The video itself flags the 10% margin as a hypothetical ('suppose... to be clear, it currently does not'), so this checks the calculator, not the world; the verdict rides on claim 9's profit figure, which is itself capped at misleading.

claim: The US has [roughly a $10 trillion] white-collar wage economy
quote: the roughly 10 trillion-dollar white-collar wage economy
evidence: No source directly confirms a $10T white-collar figure. Total US wages across all occupations were $12.3T in 2025 (BLS); a narrower 'high AI-exposure occupations' wage bill was estimated at $3.7T. $10T for the broader white-collar category (wider than just high-AI-exposure roles) sits plausibly between these two bounds but isn't independently pinned down.

claim: AI profitably capturing a tenth of the white-collar wage pool is [the equivalent] of replacing something like [10 million] American white-collar workers every year
quote: equivalent of replacing something like 10 million American white-collar workers every single year
evidence: $1T (10% of the claimed $10T pool) ÷ 10,000,000 workers implies an average replaced-worker value of ~$100K/year — a reasonable white-collar salary proxy, but never stated in the video; it's an unstated assumption baked into the headline number. Rides on claim 12's unconfirmed $10T base.

claim: Chinese AI labs, with a fraction of America's computing power, have produced open models that are by most measures [slightly behind, level with, or occasionally ahead of] the best American systems
quote: Chinese labs with a fraction of America's computing power have produced open models that are by most measures slightly behind, level with, or occasionally ahead of the best American systems
evidence: Moonshot's Kimi K3 reportedly beats a flagship US model on a coding benchmark (Frontend Code Arena) while Moonshot itself says K3 'still trails the most powerful proprietary models' overall — a genuinely mixed picture matching the hedged 'behind, level, or ahead' framing.

claim: [Moonshot AI's Kimi K3] is a model whose performance many developers reportedly find comparable to the flagship American models for everyday work
quote: a model whose performance many developers reportedly find comparable to the flagship American brains for everyday work
evidence: Kimi K3 is a real, 2.8T-parameter open-weight model (not a mis-transcription of 'K2' as initially suspected) that beats a flagship model on at least one benchmark. 'Many developers reportedly find [it] comparable... for everyday work' is a vaguer claim no single source directly measures, but it's consistent with the model's documented competitiveness.

claim: Chinese open models now [reportedly] account for [more than 60%] of all tokens used by American firms, according to OpenRouter data
quote: Chinese open models now reportedly account for more than 60% of all tokens used by American firms
evidence: OpenRouter-derived figures for mid-2026 cluster at 58-63% Chinese-model share of US enterprise token volume (record 58%, briefly 63% in early July; June 2026 rankings put it at 61%). 'More than 60%' holds for several of the cited weeks.

claim: A compressed Chinese model called [Qwen] reportedly performs on par with the American flagship models of [roughly a year earlier], running on [a machine that fits under a desk]
quote: reportedly performs on par with the American flagship models of barely a year ago on a machine that fits under a desk
evidence: Qwen models are documented as running 6-12 months behind frontier models; a specific 27B-parameter Qwen variant is described as performing 'in the same league as' a recent Anthropic flagship while running on laptop-class hardware — matching the claim closely.

claim: AI has [sometimes] made up case law [that lawyers relied on] in actual courtrooms
quote: made up the case law again. Which, cheeky detail, it sometimes did in actual courtrooms.
evidence: A public tracker documents 1,598 US court cases involving AI-fabricated citations as of June 2026, including attorney suspensions and sanctions — a well-established pattern.

claim: A recent survey of thousands of companies [reportedly] found that [over 70%] of the AI customer-service agents that went live had to be rolled back or shut down over mistakes and miscommunications
quote: A recent survey of thousands of companies reportedly found that over 70% of the AI customer service agents that went live had to be rolled back or shut down over mistakes and miscommunications
evidence: Sinch's 'AI Production Paradox' survey (May 2026, 2,527 senior AI decision-makers across 10 countries) found a 74% rollback rate for live AI customer-service agents — matches 'over 70%' and the 'thousands of companies' framing.

claim: Across the whole economy, the most optimistic estimates put genuine AI job replacement at [something under 100,000] workers a year
quote: the most optimistic estimates put genuine AI job replacement at something under 100,000 workers a year
evidence: The lowest available figure (55,000 AI-driven US job losses in 2025) sits under 100,000, supporting the claim at that point. But Goldman Sachs' April 2026 estimate of net AI displacement — the most current figure available before this video published — was roughly 192,000/year (16,000/month), already about double the claimed ceiling; AI-cited job-cut announcements alone totaled 101,743 in just the first half of 2026. 'Under 100,000' understates the most current mid-2026 estimate.

claim: 10 million jobs a year needed versus under 100,000 actually replaced is [not a rounding error]; it is [off by a factor of 100]
quote: That is not a rounding error. That is off by a factor of 100.
evidence: 10,000,000 / 100,000 = 100 — the arithmetic is correct given the video's own inputs. But since claim 20's 'under 100,000' input understates the most current (Goldman Sachs, ~192,000/year) estimate available at publication, the real gap by that yardstick is closer to 50x, not 100x. The underlying point — the shortfall is enormous — still holds either way.

claim: The AI leaders who spent years promising [the job apocalypse] have [reportedly] begun [gently, carefully] walking it back toward softer language and longer timelines
quote: the same leaders who spent years promising the job apocalypse have reportedly begun gently, carefully walking it back
evidence: Extensively reported in mid-2026: Forbes ('The Jobs Apocalypse Was Just Called Off By The People Who Predicted It,' July 25 2026) and Axios (Aug 20 2026) both document Altman, Huang and others softening rhetoric from 'job apocalypse' toward 'augmenting'/'working alongside' language.

claim: There is [a rush] toward stock-market listings by AI companies at [some of the most aggressive valuations ever attempted]
quote: there is a rush towards stock market listings at some of the most aggressive valuations ever attempted
evidence: SpaceX IPO'd June 2026 at a record $1.77T valuation; Anthropic is planning an October 2026 Nasdaq listing off a $965B private valuation; OpenAI is preparing bankers for a listing near $1T. The 12 most-watched IPO pipeline companies represent a combined $3T+, ~92% AI/AI-adjacent — described as 'the most AI-concentrated IPO year on record.'

claim: The same AI industry leaders are [reportedly] asking Washington for financial support — loan guarantees, backstops
quote: the same leaders are reportedly asking Washington for financial support, loan guarantees, backstops
evidence: Real episode: OpenAI's CFO said in November 2025 that a government 'backstop' would help financing — but retracted it within 24 hours, and Sam Altman stated 'we do not have or want government guarantees for OpenAI datacenters,' with the White House's AI czar adding there would be 'no federal bailout.' By the time this video published (July 2026), the company's stated position was the opposite of what's described; presenting this as a current, ongoing ask overstates a position retracted roughly eight months earlier.

claim: A man sitting near the narrator while fishing was made redundant [live, over speakerphone,] by an automated system, which got his name wrong twice, called him [Brenda], and offered him a discount code for the software that replaced him
quote: the man on the next chair got made redundant live over speakerphone by what was unmistakably a machine. A pleasant automated voice thanked him for his years of service, got his name wrong twice, called him Brenda once, and finished by offering him a discount code for the very software that had replaced him.
evidence: Personal anecdote about an unnamed bystander; no independent record could exist. Used illustratively, not as load-bearing evidence for the numeric thesis.
